lessons.title: Business continuity and business impact analysis (BIA)
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of an hourglass next to a failed server, with an arrow pointing back marked RPO and an arrow pointing forward marked RTO.
objectives: Tell apart the business continuity plan (BCP), the disaster recovery plan (DRP) and the incident response plan.
Carry out a business impact analysis (BIA).
Define and link MTD, RTO, RPO and WRT.
Place the main stages of a continuity program.

references.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
ISO 22301, Security and resilience: business continuity management systems

blocks.text: Three plans not to confuse

rows: BCP, business continuity plan (plan de continuité d'activité, PCA)
How does the organization keep its essential activities going during and after a crisis?
The whole organization: people, processes, premises, suppliers
DRP, disaster recovery plan (plan de reprise d'activité, PRA)
How are IT systems and data brought back into service?
Mainly technology, often at another site
How is a security incident detected, contained and handled?
Security events, often without loss of the site

blocks.text: BCP = the business carries on. DRP = IT comes back. The DRP is part of the BCP.

blocks.title: Human life first
blocks.text: In any continuity plan, people's safety comes before property, data and systems. Evacuating, sheltering and accounting for people always comes before IT recovery.
The business impact analysis

blocks.title: BIA, Business Impact Analysis (bilan d'impact sur l'activité)
blocks.text: Study that identifies essential processes, their dependencies (people, applications, suppliers, premises) and the impact of their interruption over time. It sets the recovery objectives and is the basis of all continuity strategies.

blocks.title: Steps of a BIA
items: Identify the business processes and their owners.
List the resources and dependencies of each process.
Assess the impact of an interruption over time: financial, legal, reputation, people's safety.
Set the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and derive the RTO and RPO from it.
Rank the processes by recovery priority.
Have the results approved by senior management.

blocks.text: The time indicators

rows: Maximum tolerable downtime before unacceptable damage
Payroll cannot stop for more than 72 h
Target time to bring the system back into service
Time to verify the data and resume normal work after the return to service
Maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time before the incident
Losing 4 h of data entry is accepted

blocks.title: Before and after the incident
blocks.alt: Timeline: to the left of the incident, the RPO measures how much recent data you accept to lose since the last backup; to the right, the RTO then the WRT, whose sum must remain less than or equal to the MTD.

blocks.text: Two reflexes: the RPO looks back (how much data is lost) and dictates the frequency of backups or replication; the RTO looks forward (how much downtime) and dictates the type of recovery site. And the RTO is always shorter than the MTD.
A program, not a document

blocks.title: The stages of a continuity program (based on NIST SP 800-34)
blocks.alt: Seven-stage cycle: policy, impact analysis, preventive measures, recovery strategies, plan writing, testing and training, plan maintenance, with senior management support at the center.

blocks.title: Case: the BIA workshop
blocks.text: In a fictitious online retail company, the BIA workshop shows that order taking loses €40,000 per hour of downtime and that senior management tolerates no more than 8 hours (MTD). The team sets an RTO of 4 hours, a WRT of 2 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes, which requires continuous replication of the order database. Accounting, less urgent, gets an MTD of 5 days and simple daily backups.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Senior management: I approve the MTDs, because they are risk acceptance choices.
Business owner: I know the real impact of one hour of downtime of my process.
CIO: I translate RTO and RPO into technical solutions and a budget.
Auditor: I check that the BIA is recent and approved, and that the plan follows from it.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: The BIA comes before the strategies and the plan.
RPO = data lost (past); RTO = downtime (future).
RTO + WRT ≤ MTD.
Senior management support is the first success factor.
People's safety always comes first.
BCP (business), DRP (IT), IRP (incidents).
BIA: critical processes, dependencies, impacts, priorities.
MTD, RTO, WRT, RPO and how they relate.
Continuous program supported by senior management.

lessons.title: Recovery strategies: sites, backups and redundancy
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three buildings: a hot site with servers switched on, a warm site with some equipment, and an empty cold site with only power outlets.
objectives: Compare hot, warm, cold and mobile sites, reciprocal agreement and cloud recovery.
Choose between full, incremental and differential backup.
Explain RAID levels and component redundancy.
Use MTBF and mean time to repair to reason about availability.

references.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

blocks.text: Recovery sites

rows: Hardware, network and software ready; mainly the latest data is missing
Premises, network and part of the hardware
Premises, electricity, air conditioning; no hardware
Another organization hosts in case of disaster

blocks.text: The hotter the site, the faster and more expensive it is. The RTO picks the temperature of the site.

blocks.title: Reciprocal agreements and sites too close
blocks.text: A reciprocal agreement is hard to enforce: the other organization may lack capacity or be hit by the same disaster, and confidentiality is tricky. A recovery site that is too close may suffer the same flood, the same power outage or the same earthquake zone.
Types of backup

rows: What changed since the last backup, whatever its type
Slow: the full one then all the incrementals
What changed since the last full backup
Longer and longer during the week
Medium: the full one then the last differential

blocks.text: Classic question: restore after a failure on Thursday, with a full backup on Sunday. With incrementals: the full one plus those of Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. With differentials: the full one plus only Wednesday's. Full and incremental backups reset the files' archive bit; the differential does not.

blocks.title: A backup must be tested
blocks.text: Media are kept off site, protected (encryption, access control), with at least one offline or immutable copy. Restoration is tested regularly to check that it works and fits within the RTO.
Redundancy

blocks.title: Common RAID levels
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy; RAID 1 mirrors to two disks; RAID 5 stripes with parity and survives the loss of one disk; RAID 6 uses double parity and survives the loss of two disks.

blocks.title: RAID is not a backup
blocks.text: RAID protects against the failure of a disk, not against a deletion, corruption or ransomware: the error is instantly copied to all the disks. It complements backups without replacing them.

rows: Overload and failure of a node
Short outages, long enough to shut down cleanly or start the generator
Dual power supply, dual carrier link

blocks.title: MTBF and mean time to repair
blocks.text: MTBF (mean time between failures) measures the reliability of a component; mean time to repair (often written MTTR, Mean Time To Repair) measures the time to restore it. Availability ≈ MTBF / (MTBF + repair time). Be careful: in a SOC, MTTR rather means the mean time to respond to an incident.

blocks.title: Case: choosing the site
blocks.text: A fictitious mutual insurer has an RTO of 4 hours for its reimbursement service and 15 days for its archives. It rents a hot site in another region for reimbursements, with replication every 15 minutes, and a shared cold site for the archives. The hot site is chosen more than 100 km away so as not to depend on the same power grid.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CIO: RTO and RPO tell me which solution to buy; without them I oversize or undersize.
CFO: a mirror site is expensive, so it must protect a process that justifies it.
Auditor: I ask for proof of the last restore test.
Operator: I monitor backups every day; a failed backup must raise an alert.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Hot site = hours; warm = days; cold = weeks.
Incremental: fast backup, slow restore; differential: the opposite.
RAID 0 offers no redundancy; RAID 5 = at least 3 disks.
RAID does not replace backup.
Reciprocal agreement: cheap but hard to enforce.
Sites: mirror, hot, warm, cold, mobile, reciprocal, cloud.
Backups: full, incremental, differential; off-site storage, tests.
Redundancy: RAID, clusters, load balancing, power.
Availability: MTBF and repair time.

lessons.title: Writing, testing and maintaining the plan
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a table on which lie a "Business continuity plan" binder, a stopwatch and scenario cards, with an "exercise" checkbox.
objectives: List the expected contents of a continuity and recovery plan.
Organize the teams and crisis communication.
Compare the five types of tests, from the least to the most risky.
Keep the plan up to date and use lessons learned.

references.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities

blocks.text: What the plan contains

blocks.title: Typical contents
items: Objectives, scope and assumptions (from the BIA).
Criteria and authority to declare a disaster and activate the plan.
Teams, roles, alternates and up-to-date contact details.
Recovery procedures in order of priority, with RTO and RPO.
Communication plan: staff, customers, authorities, media, with a designated spokesperson.
Procedure for returning to the primary site.
Appendices: inventories, supplier contracts, configurations.

rows: Decides, declares the disaster, arbitrates, communicates
Brings services back at the recovery site, in order of priority
Assesses the damage and restores the primary site

blocks.title: Returning to the primary site
blocks.text: The return is prepared like a recovery: the least critical functions go back first, to check that the primary site is safe and stable, then the most critical ones are switched over. The disaster is only over when normal activity has resumed at the primary site.
Testing the plan

blocks.title: Tests, from the lightest to the most risky
blocks.alt: Five-step scale: checklist review, tabletop exercise (also called structured walk-through), simulation, parallel test at the recovery site, then full interruption of production, the most risky.

nodes.label: Tabletop exercise
nodes.detail: the scenario is walked through together

nodes.label: Simulation
nodes.detail: scenario played out, without stopping production

nodes.label: Parallel
nodes.detail: systems started at the recovery site, production maintained

blocks.title: The full interruption
blocks.text: Stopping production to really switch over is the most realistic and most risky test: it can cause the disaster it aims to prevent. It requires written approval from senior management, solid preparation and a planned rollback.

In the exam: the checklist review is the least costly; the tabletop exercise brings the teams together around the scenario; the parallel test starts the recovery site without cutting production; the full interruption is the most risky and requires senior management approval.
Maintaining the plan

blocks.title: Keeping the plan alive
items: Review it at least once a year and at every major change: new application, move, supplier, reorganization.
Update contact details and alternates.
Train newcomers and raise awareness among all staff.
After every test or real incident, write up lessons learned and correct the plan.
Include plan updates in change management.
Keep copies off site and accessible even without the information system.

blocks.text: An untested plan is a hypothesis; a plan that is not updated is a trap.

blocks.title: Case: the tabletop exercise
blocks.text: During a simulated tabletop exercise, the facilitator announces the flooding of the basement that houses the server room. While walking through the plan, the team discovers that the on-call number of the recovery site provider has changed and that the procedure assumes access to the network share… which is in the flooded room. Both corrections are made the following week and a paper copy of the plan is placed at each site.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Senior management: I chair the crisis unit and approve risky tests.
Continuity manager: I plan a progressive test program over the year.
Communication: I prepare template messages for customers and the press in advance.
Auditor: I compare the date of the last test and the last plan update with recent changes.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Order of tests: checklist, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption.
Full interruption = senior management approval.
Return to the primary site: least critical functions first.
The plan must be accessible without the information system.
Any significant change to the IS triggers an update of the plan.
Plan: activation, teams, priorities, communication, return.
Progressive tests; full interruption reserved and approved.
Maintenance: annual review, changes, lessons learned, training.
Off-site and offline copies.

flashcards.back: Business continuity / IT recovery; the DRP is part of the BCP.
The safety of people.
Critical processes, dependencies, impacts over time; comes before the strategies.
Maximum tolerable downtime.
Time to bring the system back into service; drives the choice of site.
Acceptable data loss; sets the backup frequency.
Time to verify and resume work; RTO + WRT ≤ MTD.
Hours / days / weeks.
Cheap, unreliable, hard to enforce.
Quick to take; restore the full backup + all the incrementals.
Restore the full backup + the latest differential.
Striping with no redundancy / mirroring.
Parity, 1 disk (min. 3) / double parity, 2 disks.
A deletion or an encryption is copied everywhere.
Mean time between failures; availability ≈ MTBF / (MTBF + repair time).
Short outage / long outage.
Checklist review, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption.
The riskiest; requires management approval.
The least critical functions first.
Annual review, major changes, lessons learned, off-site copies.

revisionSheet: # Revision sheet: business continuity and recovery
BCP: continuity of the whole business; DRP: bringing systems and data back into service (part of the BCP); IRP: response to security incidents.
Top priority: the safety of people. First success factor: management support.
BIA first: critical processes, dependencies, impacts over time, priorities, approval by management.
MTD (tolerable downtime), RTO (back in service), WRT (work resumed), RPO (data lost); RTO + WRT ≤ MTD.
RPO → frequency of backups or replication; RTO → type of site and solution.
Sites: mirror (immediate), hot (hours), warm (days), cold (weeks), mobile, reciprocal agreement (unreliable), cloud; keep the backup site at a distance.
Backups: full; incremental (fast, restore = full + all of them); differential (restore = full + the latest); off-site, protected, tested.
RAID 0 (no redundancy), 1 (mirroring), 5 (parity, 1 disk, min. 3), 6 (double parity, 2 disks), 10; RAID is not a backup.
Redundancy: clusters and failover, load balancing, UPS, generator, dual power supplies and links.
Plan: activation and authority, teams and alternates, priorities, communication (spokesperson), return to the primary site (least critical first).
Tests: checklist review, tabletop exercise, simulation, parallel, full interruption (management approval).
Maintenance: annual review and at each major change, lessons learned, training, off-site and offline copies.
Pairs not to confuse: BCP/DRP; RTO/RPO; incremental/differential; RAID/backup; parallel/full interruption.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a BCP and a DRP?
choices: The DRP covers the whole organization, and the BCP only IT
The BCP only concerns fires, the DRP all other crises
The BCP covers all business activity; the DRP, IT recovery
They are two synonyms for exactly the same document
questions.explanation: The DRP is a technical component of the BCP.

whyNot.0: It is the other way around.
whyNot.1: The BCP covers every type of disaster.

questions.prompt: What is the absolute priority in a continuity plan?
questions.explanation: Human life comes before property, data and systems.

questions.prompt: Which activity must be carried out before choosing recovery strategies?
questions.explanation: The BIA sets the priorities and objectives (MTD, RTO, RPO) from which the strategies follow.

whyNot.1: A site is chosen only once the RTO is known.

questions.prompt: Management agrees to lose at most 2 hours of data entry. Which metric does this set?
questions.explanation: The RPO is the acceptable data loss, measured in time; here it requires a backup or replication at least every 2 hours.

whyNot.1: The MTD is the tolerable downtime.
whyNot.3: The RTO is the time to restore service.

questions.prompt: Which relationship must hold between RTO, WRT and MTD?
questions.explanation: The time to restore service plus the time to resume work must not exceed the maximum tolerable downtime.

whyNot.2: The MTD is the upper bound.
whyNot.3: The WRT is only part of the MTD.

questions.prompt: A process has an RTO of 2 hours. Which decision does this figure mainly guide?
choices: The type of recovery site and solution
questions.explanation: A short RTO requires a fast recovery solution (hot site, replication, failover).

whyNot.0: It is the RPO that sets the backup frequency.

questions.prompt: What is the most important factor for the success of a continuity program?
choices: The number of pages in the plan
questions.explanation: Management sets the priorities, approves the MTDs and allocates the resources.

whyNot.3: A long plan is not an effective plan.

questions.prompt: During a BIA, which elements must be identified for each critical process? (several answers)
choices: The impact of the interruption over time
The dependencies: applications, people, suppliers, premises
questions.explanation: The BIA links processes, dependencies, impacts and recovery objectives.

questions.prompt: The MTD for invoicing is 48 h and the WRT is estimated at 12 h. What is the maximum RTO that can be set?
questions.explanation: RTO + WRT ≤ MTD, so RTO ≤ 48 − 12 = 36 h.

questions.prompt: A phishing attack compromises three accounts, with no loss of site or system. Which plan applies first?
choices: The disaster recovery plan at the backup site
questions.explanation: A security incident without a disaster falls under incident response; the BCP can be activated if the impact worsens.

whyNot.1: A plan exists for this case.

questions.prompt: Which backup site already has the hardware, network and software, and can take over within a few hours?
questions.explanation: The hot site is ready; what is mainly missing is the latest data.

whyNot.0: The cold site only has the premises and power.

questions.prompt: Which site is the cheapest but the slowest to make operational?
questions.explanation: It only provides the premises, electricity and air conditioning: everything has to be installed.

questions.prompt: Full backup on Sunday, incremental backups Monday to Saturday. Failure on Thursday morning. What must be restored?
choices: The full backup, then only Wednesday's incremental
The full backup, then Monday's, Tuesday's and Wednesday's incrementals
questions.explanation: Each incremental only contains the changes since the previous backup: the whole chain is needed.

whyNot.0: That would be the case with differentials.
whyNot.3: The base and the previous days would be missing.

questions.prompt: Full backup on Sunday, differential backups every day. Failure on Thursday morning. What must be restored?
choices: The full backup, then Wednesday's differential
The full backup, then all the differentials
questions.explanation: The differential contains all the changes since the last full backup.

whyNot.3: Unnecessary: the latest one contains the earlier ones.

questions.prompt: Which RAID level offers no redundancy?
questions.explanation: RAID 0 stripes data for performance: losing one disk loses everything.

questions.prompt: How many disks can fail at the same time without data loss in RAID 6?
questions.explanation: Double parity tolerates the loss of two disks.

questions.prompt: Why does RAID 1 not protect against ransomware?
choices: Because RAID 1 itself encrypts the data it stores
Because RAID 1 is always offline, and therefore never up to date
Because RAID 1 actually has only one disk
Because the encryption is copied onto both disks
questions.explanation: RAID protects against hardware failure, not against a logical change; backups are needed.

whyNot.2: It has at least two disks.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of a reciprocal agreement between two companies?
choices: It has no drawback if it is signed by both management teams
It costs more than a fully dedicated mirror site
It is hard to enforce and capacity may be lacking
It is prohibited by law between two private companies
questions.explanation: Cheap, but unreliable: capacity, confidentiality, a disaster affecting both.

whyNot.1: On the contrary, it is inexpensive.

questions.prompt: A device has an MTBF of 990 hours and a mean time to repair of 10 hours. What is its approximate availability?

whyNot.1: That would require a repair time of about 1 hour.

questions.prompt: Which device supplies power during a short outage, long enough to start the generator?
questions.explanation: The UPS covers minutes; the generator covers long outages.

whyNot.3: Protects the disks, not the power.

questions.prompt: Which test is the least costly and the least risky?
choices: Simulating a disaster with the teams
The parallel test at the backup site
questions.explanation: Everyone rereads their part of the plan, without involving any systems.

questions.prompt: Which test brings up the systems at the backup site while production continues at the primary site?
questions.explanation: It checks the backup site without stopping business operations.

questions.prompt: What must be obtained before a full interruption test?
choices: Nothing in particular, it is a test
The opinion of the main customers
A new antivirus at the backup site
questions.explanation: It is the riskiest test: it can cause a real interruption.

whyNot.0: Such a test requires formal approval.

questions.prompt: How does a tabletop exercise (or walk-through) work?
choices: The teams meet and work through a scenario together, step by step
The power to the primary data center is actually cut
All the backups are restored directly into production
Everyone reads their part of the plan alone at home, without a meeting
questions.explanation: It reveals inconsistencies and gaps with no risk to production.

whyNot.1: That would be a real interruption.

questions.prompt: When returning to the primary site, which functions are moved back first?
choices: All of them at the same time
None, everything stays at the backup site
questions.explanation: The stability of the primary site is checked with the least sensitive functions before the critical ones are brought back.

whyNot.0: Vital functions would be put at risk on an unproven site.
whyNot.2: The backup site is not meant to last.

questions.prompt: Which event must trigger an update of the continuity plan?
choices: The arrival of an intern with no role in the plan
The deployment of a new critical application
questions.explanation: Any major change to the information system, the premises or the organization must be reflected in the plan.

questions.prompt: Why keep copies of the plan off-site and outside the information system?
choices: Because the disaster can make the plan inaccessible
To reduce the number of pages of the plan kept on the server
To comply with the company's brand guidelines and archiving
Because the plan is confidential and must be destroyed after each test
questions.explanation: A plan stored only on the server hit by the disaster is useless.

whyNot.3: It must be protected, not destroyed.

questions.prompt: Who should have the authority to declare a disaster and activate the plan?
choices: A designated member of management (and their deputies)
Any employee who witnesses the disaster
The media, once the disaster is made public
questions.explanation: Activation commits costs and decisions: the authority and the criteria are defined in advance.

whyNot.0: It carries out the contract; it does not decide.

questions.prompt: Why appoint a single spokesperson in the crisis communication plan?
choices: To replace the crisis team with a single person
Because the law prohibits other employees from speaking
So that nobody else in the company is informed
questions.explanation: A consistent message protects the company's image and avoids leaks or mistakes.

whyNot.0: The spokesperson is part of the crisis team.

questions.prompt: Which actions follow a test of the plan? (several answers)
choices: Training people on the weak points
Deleting the results to avoid the audit
Correcting the plan based on the gaps found
questions.explanation: The test is there to improve: lessons learned, correction, training.

whyNot.1: The results are evidence that is useful for the audit.
